comment: Baseline rules embedded into the Sentinel binary via include_bytes!. The eventual remote rules file at rules-v1.json will follow the same schema. Rules can be added here without code changes; behavior (conditions, apply, state checks) is restricted to the named kinds defined in Rust.

rules.title: Enable Windows Game Mode
rules.description: Game Mode tells Windows to prioritize the foreground game, deprioritize background updates, and pause Windows Update reboots while you're playing.

rules.title: Trim Windows visual effects
rules.description: Animations, transparency, and shadow effects look nice but cost a few percent of GPU and CPU. Setting the 'best performance' preset turns most off; some apply immediately, the rest on your next sign-in.
rules.impact: Snappier UI · slightly higher in-game FPS
rules.downside: UI looks more utilitarian — no fade animations.

rules.title: Disable mouse acceleration ('Enhance pointer precision')
rules.description: Windows applies a non-linear acceleration curve to mouse movement by default — the same physical motion produces different cursor distances depending on how fast you move. Off = 1:1 movement, which is what every competitive shooter expects and what aim-training builds muscle memory around.
rules.impact: Consistent aim · predictable flicks · removes a hidden variable
rules.downside: If you've gotten used to acceleration for desktop use, the cursor will feel slower at first — you may want to bump DPI / sensitivity to compensate.

rules.title: Disable Game Bar and Game DVR
rules.description: Game Bar's background capture and Game DVR (Windows' built-in recording layer) add CPU and disk overhead in every running game whether you use them or not. Most users have third-party capture (OBS, ShadowPlay, AMD ReLive) and never touch Windows' version. Turning it off frees up resources.
rules.impact: Lower background overhead in every game
rules.downside: You'll lose the Win+G overlay and Windows' built-in clip recording.

rules.title: Disable Windows telemetry (DiagTrack)
rules.description: DiagTrack ('Connected User Experiences and Telemetry') runs in the background sending usage and diagnostic data to Microsoft. Disabling it has no functional impact on day-to-day use but does mean some of the data Windows uses to detect crashes and roll back broken updates won't be sent.
rules.impact: Less background network traffic · less idle CPU · privacy
rules.downside: Windows feedback submissions and automatic update-rollback diagnostics rely on this service. Most users never notice.

rules.title: Disable Windows Search indexer (HDD-only systems)
rules.description: On systems with only spinning hard drives, the Windows Search service (WSearch) constantly indexes files and causes meaningful disk thrash that you can hear and feel. On NVMe / SSD systems the indexing cost is small and the speed savings are real, so Sentinel hides this recommendation entirely unless every detected drive is an HDD.
rules.impact: Lower idle disk activity · less HDD thrash · ~50–150 MB RAM back
rules.downside: Start menu / File Explorer search becomes slower and less complete — it falls back to live filesystem walking instead of pre-built indexes. You can re-enable any time.

rules.title: Disable Nagle's Algorithm (advanced — TCP-heavy games only)
rules.description: Nagle's Algorithm batches small TCP packets together to save bandwidth at the cost of a few ms of latency. This tweak is widely recommended in gaming guides, but most modern games run over UDP, not TCP — disabling Nagle does nothing for them. It can help in games that genuinely use TCP for gameplay traffic (some MMORPGs, certain older titles, some emulators), and is otherwise advanced-mode territory.
rules.impact: Lower latency in games that actually use TCP for gameplay traffic
rules.downside: Marginally more network overhead. For UDP-based games (which is most of them today), this does nothing.
rules.applies_to_template: Active network adapter — verify your specific game uses TCP before enabling
